content:
Dozens of pages from the President's Daily Brief were declassified on Friday, coinciding with the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks. The documents detail the intelligence collected by government officials about bin Laden and al-Qaeda before the hijackings — an attack that killed nearly 3,000 people and fundamentally reshaped America's national security landscape.

The documents show how security analysts tracked bin Laden's movements and support networks, along with concerns about possible threats to US targets. They also detail officials' understanding of his networks in the United States and other countries, including how his operations were funded.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe described the move as an act of "unprecedented transparency" and said the documents represented the largest single batch of declassified President's Daily Briefs in the agency's history. The President's Daily Brief is a highly classified intelligence document prepared by the intelligence community for the government's top leadership.

The documents span from February 1998 — a brief presented to then-President Clinton titled "Terrorist Seeking Weapons of Mass Destruction Capability," which mentioned bin Laden and other Islamic extremists — to September 12, 2001, the day after the attacks, in which sources indicated the plot had been planned for two years and that the US Capitol had at one point been considered as a target.

An April 1998 document described the Taliban's reluctance to hand over bin Laden, who was viewed as their "guest" in Afghanistan, noting that the Taliban "remained grateful for his assistance during the Soviet occupation" and were "unwilling to jeopardize their relationship with him by surveilling or restricting his activities."

A July 1998 brief stated that "bin Laden is likely to have considered attacks on the US homeland a high priority" and noted that he "was interested in using chemical and biological weapons to mount attacks."

Two months later, a briefer wrote that bin Laden's "preferred tactic was to mount attacks on the US soil in Washington," and that al-Qaeda "could fly an aircraft loaded with explosives into a US city."

Potential hijackings were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described how the planners "evaded security checks during a trial run at an unspecified New York airport," and noted that "members of bin Laden's network had received training in hijacking."

Other documents detail bin Laden's efforts to acquire materials for a so-called dirty bomb — a conventional weapon combined with radioactive material. By June 1999, intelligence officials indicated his operatives had conducted related explosive experiments to "enhance the blast's destructive power."

About two years before the attacks, intelligence officials observed that bin Laden appeared to be misleading the Taliban about his intentions to strike the United States without provocation. Briefings prepared for President George W. Bush in early 2001 focused in part on bin Laden's "rudimentary efforts to develop and deploy biological weapons."

A report one month before the attacks stated that bin Laden was "committed to carrying out terrorist attacks against the United States," and noted that the 1998 al-Qaeda bombings of US embassies "demonstrated that he was willing to take years to plan an operation and was undeterred by setbacks."

At the time — in August 2001 — officials wrote that "there were suspicious activities in the United States consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York," adding that the FBI "was conducting approximately 70 full field investigations throughout the United States that it considered to be bin Laden-related."

Many of the documents were redacted to hide the names of sources and other identifying details. The documents did not appear to yield any significant new breakthroughs regarding the planning of the attacks or how US officials understood the events.

In the years following the attacks, a bipartisan commission pointed to a lack of intelligence sharing between agencies such as the CIA and the FBI, and issued recommendations that led to the creation of new positions, including the Director of National Intelligence and the National Counterterrorism Center, which is responsible for analyzing terrorism intelligence across government departments both at home and abroad.

When asked about the response to the latest declassified documents, the White House pointed to the National Archives' separate release of another batch of documents the same day, including transcripts of interviews with national security officials from the Clinton and Bush administrations. Those documents were the product of a commission that investigated the attacks between 2002 and 2004.
